key_insight: Ly and Gong propose that deep learning’s unpredictability stems from fractal basin geometry: starting points that lead to different outcomes are interwoven at arbitrarily fine scales. Greater precision may therefore offer little improvement in predicting the final outcome.
problem_solved: Addresses why deep learning outcomes can remain difficult to predict and reproduce, even when starting conditions are controlled with increasing precision.
method: Frame training outcomes in terms of basins: sets of starting points that lead to the same outcome.
Propose that basins for different outcomes have fractal geometry, interweaving at arbitrarily fine scales.
Connect this geometry to limits on how much increased starting-point precision can improve predictability and reproducibility.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, tighter control of initialization may not guarantee consistent outcomes. The proposed mechanism highlights the importance of assessing variability across runs rather than relying on a single training result.
visual_elements: Color-coded basin map showing nearby starting points leading to different outcomes.
Nested zoom panels illustrating how outcome regions remain interwoven at finer scales.
Conceptual chart showing limited predictability gains as starting-point precision increases.
Two training trajectories starting nearly together and ending at different outcomes.
paper_title: Fractal basin geometry and the limits to predictability and reproducibility in deep learning
